logline: A child born without body parts - sacrificed by his warlord father to twelve demon gods - wanders feudal Japan reclaiming his own flesh one demon at a time, guided by an orphan thief named Dororo.

renewal.note: The 24-episode single-season run concluded in June 2019. MAPPA and Tezuka Productions have not announced a continuation. The manga's original ending was adapted with modifications.

seasons.review_body: Dororo premiered on Tokyo MX in January 2019, a MAPPA and Tezuka Productions adaptation of Osamu Tezuka's 1967 manga. Anime News Network's Lauren Orsini awarded it a B+ after three episodes, calling it a contender for 2019's anime of the year and praising the modernized visual language - limited color palette, watercolor washes, and a reimagined Hyakkimaru who communicates entirely through sensing life forces rather than speech. The 4th Crunchyroll Anime Awards recognized it with the Best Character Design award. ANN later placed it among the best MAPPA series of all time. Some critics noted the episodic second half lost momentum relative to the focused first half, but the character work on Hyakkimaru and Dororo's relationship was consistently cited as exceptional.

episode_reviews.title: The Story of Daigo
episode_reviews.review_body: Dororo's premiere is MAPPA's adaptation of Osamu Tezuka's 1967 manga, and the studio makes the visual register immediately its own: prosthetic limbs against Sengoku-era Japan, a muted palette broken by demon silhouettes, a protagonist whose entire sensory world was sold before he was born. The episode establishes the premise in its most brutal form - Lord Daigo's pact with twelve demons, the newborn sacrificed to grant him land and power, the resulting creature that survives and grows into Hyakkimaru - without softening the originating horror. Anime News Network identified the series as 'a contender for 2019's anime of the year after just three episodes,' and the premiere established the visual grammar that justified the assessment: the specific way MAPPA renders Hyakkimaru's perceptual world, where he cannot see, hear, or feel in human terms but perceives demons and other living beings through their spiritual presence.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes the series' premise in its most brutal form: a warlord's pact, a newborn sacrificed to twelve demons, and the resulting creature that grows into Hyakkimaru. MAPPA's visual design - prosthetic limbs against Sengoku-era Japan, a muted palette broken by demon silhouettes - is immediately arresting.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The moment Hyakkimaru first sees Dororo's aura as living light - the sensory world of a person who perceives differently.

episode_reviews.title: The Story of Bandai
episode_reviews.review_body: Dororo Episode 12 is the midseason episode that deepens the series' co-protagonist's backstory and begins closing the emotional distance between the two leads. The series' most consistent formal achievement is in knowing when to pause the episodic demon-hunting for the question that underlies it: what Hyakkimaru is actually recovering when he reclaims each body part from the demons, and what he loses in the process. Episode 12 works because it makes Dororo's history with Itachi - which had been telegraphed across earlier episodes - the subject of an episode rather than a detail, and the result is that the character the show had positioned as comic relief reveals a grief and a motive that reframes the entire preceding dynamic. The episode turns a sidekick into a fully realised character and clarifies what the series' emotional stakes actually are.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The midseason episode that deepens Dororo's backstory and begins closing the distance between the two protagonists' emotional registers. The series is at its best when the episodic demon-hunting gives way to the question of what Hyakkimaru is recovering - and what he loses with each body part reclaimed.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dororo's full history with Itachi - the episode that turns a comic sidekick into a fully realized character.

episode_reviews.title: The Story of Dororo and Hyakkimaru
episode_reviews.review_body: Dororo's series finale resolves Hyakkimaru's quest and his relationship with his father Daigo in a modified version of Tezuka's original ending - a choice that honoured the source material while acknowledging twenty-four episodes of accumulated character investment that the original manga's era did not have. Anime News Network's reviewer noted that 'after all the chips fall, our two protagonists' lives drift into a big question mark' - a description that captures both what some found earned (the ambiguity as truthful to what a life reclaimed from demons would actually look like) and what others found incomplete (a conclusion that declines to resolve the moral stakes it spent the season establishing). Hyakkimaru's choice about his reclaimed humanity - the episode's central act - carries the weight the series had been building toward, and the question of what survival costs is answered honestly rather than consolingly.
